query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the as‐manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy, degradation under elevated-temperature oxidizing exposure is governed by the formation and adhesion quality of a superficially grown oxide scale. In the baseline alloy, rapid grain boundary diffusion of oxidation‐prone elements (especially Cr and Ti) leads to the nucleation of non‐protective, poorly adherent oxides that promote local intergranular degradation. Incorporating a trace level of yttrium (Y) will modify the oxide scale formation by segregating to grain boundaries, enhancing oxide adherence and coherence, and thereby reducing the degradation rate without compromising the FCC matrix integrity and the alloy’s formability, strength, and fatigue performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy produced by an AM process with a single-phase FCC matrix.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled trace addition of yttrium (e.g., 0.1 atomic percent) during the additive manufacturing process while keeping all other composition and processing parameters unchanged.
generation.conditions: Expose both the baseline and Y-doped samples to an elevated-temperature oxidizing environment (e.g., 900 °C under a controlled oxygen partial pressure) for a defined duration. Post-exposure evaluations include oxide scale morphology (via microscopy), oxidation mass gain measurements, and mechanical property tests (tensile and fatigue) under conditions similar to those defined in the service regime.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure and adhesion quality of the oxide scale, particularly at grain boundaries where oxidation-induced degradation initiates.
generation.mechanism: Trace Y addition is expected to segregate at the grain boundaries and interface with the developing oxide scale, altering the oxidation kinetics and local diffusion pathways. This results in the formation of a more cohesive and adherent oxide layer that limits the propagation of intergranular microcracks and embrittlement, thereby retarding overall degradation during high-temperature oxidizing exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the Y-doped alloy will show a lower oxidation mass gain and exhibit a more continuous, adherent oxide scale. Consequently, its mechanical properties (e.g., tensile strength and fatigue performance) will be better preserved after oxidation exposure. The direction of change is a reduction in degradation effects; however, the precise magnitude of improvement remains uncertain until measured.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy without any Y addition, exposed under identical oxidizing conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to elevated-temperature exposures (e.g., at 900 °C) in oxidizing atmospheres with defined oxygen partial pressures and exposure durations typical for service testing of protective coatings on high-entropy alloys. It is assumed that the additive manufacturing process produces a homogeneous FCC matrix in both cases.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvement in oxidation resistance and mechanical property retention due to trace Y addition is not precisely known; the magnitude of change and long-term scale stability need experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples using additive manufacturing: one set of the baseline Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy and one set with an identical formulation except for a 0.1 at.% Y addition. Subject both sets to the same high-temperature oxidizing exposure (e.g., 900 °C in a controlled oxygen atmosphere for 120 hours). After exposure, perform a comparative analysis of the oxide scale using microscopy (to assess morphology and adhesion), measure the oxidation mass gain, and evaluate the mechanical properties (tensile and fatigue tests) of each set.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and adhesion (via SEM/TEM)
Post-exposure tensile strength and fatigue performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation mass gain, improved oxide scale adhesion and morphology, and superior retention of mechanical properties compared to the baseline alloy under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis that trace Y addition enhances oxidation resistance by stabilizing the oxide scale is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Among notable RHEA systems, the NbMoTaW and VNbMoTaW alloys demonstrate exceptional high-temperature mechanical performance, maintaining compressive strengths exceeding 400 MPa at 1600 °C [,,]. Compared to the significant yield strength reduction (>40%) observed in conventional high-temperature alloys from room temperature to 600 °C, RHEAs exhibit a much smaller strength degradation of only 20–40%, owing to their unique solid solution strengthening and sluggish diffusion effects [,,]. It should be noted that RHEAs lack sufficient oxidation resistance at elevated temperatures [,,], which limits their prospects for long-term use in practical applications. Consequently, significant efforts have been dedicated to identifying effective approaches to enhance the high-temperature oxidation performance of RHEAs [,,,,]. Among various technological approaches, microalloying has emerged as an effective strategy to balance the comprehensive properties of alloys. Lu et al. [] demonstrated the efficacy of Y microalloying in AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr RHEAs, where Y-doping was shown to suppress refractory element volatilization during oxidation and improve oxide scale adherence.
